metadata.note: The Delaware and Hudson's Pennsylvania Division -- the anthracite end of the Bridge Line, and the part of the system the repo had no line for at all. The D&H began here: its Gravity Railroad, authorized by Pennsylvania on Apr 8 1826, hauled Wurts family anthracite from Carbondale over the Moosic Mountains to the canal head at Honesdale, and on Aug 8 1829 the Stourbridge Lion became the first locomotive to run on rails in the United States. Steam replaced all of it: the Jefferson Branch, chartered 1864 and built by the Erie, opened Carbondale to Lanesboro on Oct 28 1870 and gave the D&H its first through rail route to Albany via the Erie and the Albany and Susquehanna; the Lackawanna and Susquehanna, chartered 1867 and opened 1872, shortened it by running from Nineveh straight down to Lanesboro; the Valley Road carried the traffic on down the Lackawanna from Carbondale to Scranton; and from 1886 the main line reached Wilkes-Barre. Ninety-three miles, Wilkes-Barre to Nineveh. The gravity railroad closed Jan 3 1899 and its alignment was rebuilt as the steam Honesdale Branch, a resort line to Farview Park and Lake Lodore that peaked before 1917 and shut at midnight on Sep 9 1931. Passenger service over the division itself ended in January 1952, one engineer taking the last train out in each direction. See albany_and_susquehanna_railroad.geojson for the New York half of the Bridge Line and scranton_railroads.geojson for the DL&W and CNJ at Scranton.

metadata.not_yet_sourced: The Valley Road's own opening date is the main gap: passenger service west of Carbondale is documented from 1860 and the gravity railroad reached Scranton in 1863, but on the gravity alignment, which is not the track drawn here, and no date has been found for the steam line that replaced it -- 1870 is used as a defensible floor, not a sourced date. Likewise the construction dates of the Union Coal Company and Northern Coal and Iron Company trackage between Scranton and Wilkes-Barre are unsourced; 1886 is the sourced date for D&H passenger service reaching Wilkes-Barre. Sources disagree on the Jefferson Branch: Wikipedia says built 1869 and opened 1872, while Powell, citing contemporary Carbondale newspapers, gives Oct 28 1870, which is used here because the same source has the through Albany connection working in 1871. Headways are estimates everywhere except 1898-1917, which is derived from a train count in the Jul 3 1898 timetable rather than a printed headway, and applied to the Honesdale branch only qualitatively. January 1952 is dated exactly for the Scranton-Carbondale trains but only as 'the same shutdown' for Wilkes-Barre and Nineveh. The gravity railroad's own alignment, the many colliery branches (Bull Run, Plymouth No. 5, Poplar Street, the Plymouth and Wilkes-Barre Railroad and Bridge), and the 1915 Wilkes-Barre Connecting Railroad are not drawn. Wikipedia's D&H article dates the canal's last use to Nov 5 1891 while other accounts say Nov 5 1898; the conflict is not resolved here and the canal is not drawn.

segments.note: Chartered 1864, financed by the D&H and built by the Erie Railroad, the Jefferson Branch from Carbondale to Lanesboro and the Erie main line opened Oct 28 1870. In 1871 it gave the D&H what it had wanted since the 1820s -- a direct rail connection from its Lackawanna Valley mines to Albany, running over the Erie to Binghamton and then over the Albany and Susquehanna. The Jefferson (and through it the Erie) held trackage rights over the D&H between its two sections, and the D&H held rights to Lanesboro. Frequency estimated/unsourced

Engineer Lewis Davis piloted the last Carbondale-Nineveh passenger train, in the same January 1952 shutdown. The line was abandoned in 1986 after the Belden Hill tunnel was enlarged. segments.note: The Delaware and Hudson Gravity Railroad -- whose Stourbridge Lion had made the first locomotive run on rails in the United States on Aug 8 1829 -- was ordered closed on Oct 28 1898 and ran for the last time on Jan 3 1899. Its surviving alignment (Farview to Shepherd's Crook to Lookout Junction to Carbondale, the loaded track from Farview to Waymart, and Waymart to Honesdale) was rebuilt as a standard-gauge steam line, the Honesdale Branch. Farview Park opened for the season on May 30 1899 and the D&H carried over 2,000 people up to it in about thirty widened former gravity cars fitted with glass fronts against the cinders; the branch was expected to be fully equipped with its large yellow coaches by Jan 1 1900, with a through car each way between Honesdale and Wilkes-Barre from early January. The branch was at its peak from 1899 until America entered the war in 1917, with summer trains to Lake Lodore doing heavy business. Frequency estimated/unsourced
